title: The Finch Prize

pages.text:
*The Nineteenth Rule of Mapmaking: The best prize is the distance you have come.*

Guildmaster Quint rose. The scraping of his chair was the loudest sound in the room, sharper than the gulls outside, sharper than the wind rattling the high panes. He adjusted the silver compass on his chain, and the metal clicked against his doublet.

"The Royal Chartery," he said, his voice rolling over the heads of the crowd, "is awarded to the finest craft. That place goes to Lucan Ravel."

A murmur swept through the hall. Lucan stood. His face was pale, but his spine was straight as a measuring rod. He bowed deeply, his gold compass swinging against his chest.

"However," Quint continued, and the word hung in the air, heavy and cold, "the judges have noted a discrepancy in the Greywater marsh. The map you submitted shows a meadow. The ground, as we all know, is mud. You are to re-draw that section. You are to walk it first. Then, and only then, will the place be yours."

Lucan straightened. His ears were pink, the color of the crier’s hat, but his chin was lifted.

"I would be honored," he said.
pages.image: Lucan Ravel, a boy in a green coat with silver buttons, bows deeply before a tall Guildmaster in a grey robe; his face is pale but his posture is rigid, a gold compass visible on a chain.

pages.text:
Quint turned back to the judges, but his eyes drifted to the corner of the room. He paused, a long, deliberate beat, while the dust motes danced in the slant of afternoon light.

"Fifty years ago," Quint said, "a young woman argued before this Guild that skill is not the highest measure of a mapmaker. She said that improvement is the true craft. She was laughed out of this room. Today, we are correcting that error."

He reached into his robe and pulled out a small, silver case. It was not a medal. It was a pen, slender and bright, engraved with a simple, twisting line.

"We name this the Finch Prize. It is for the greatest distance traveled between the first day and the last. For the one who drew the straightest line not with their hand, but with their heart."

Quint looked past the crowd, past the judges, until his gaze locked onto a tall, thin woman in a lavender scarf.

"It goes to Tamsin Marrow."
pages.image: The Guildmaster holds a small, ornate silver pen case up to the light, his expression solemn and proud, while the blurred background shows the crowded Guild Hall and a figure in a lavender scarf watching intently.

pages.text:
The hall erupted, a sound like the river slamming against the Lowtide pilings. It was not polite applause. It was a roar, thick and wet, filling the rafters. Odd whooped so loudly that a pigeon, startled from the beams, shot down into the middle of the room and flapped its wings in utter confusion, looking for a branch that was not there. Sixpence, safe in her basket, cooed indignantly and puffed out her white chest patch.

Tam could not breathe, because her lungs had apparently forgotten their job.

A steward placed the silver pen in her hand. It was cold, then warm, and then it was just part of her, settling into her palm like a key. The scroll was unrolled on the table. The Guild would publish her map as the official chart of the Marches. Tamsin Marrow and Odd Brannock.

Odd stared at the scroll, his gap-toothed grin gone, his eyes wide and unblinking, fixed on the ink.

"My name," he whispered.

He sat down, though he had not meant to, for his legs simply stopped working and he dropped to the marble floor with a thump that echoed in the sudden silence.
pages.image: Odd Brannock, a lanky boy with red hair and a gap-toothed grin, sits on the polished marble floor of the Guild Hall, staring in shock at a rolled scroll, while a grey pigeon flaps its wings nearby.

pages.text:
Lucan, ever the gentleman, offered his arm to Master Finch. She took it, her hawthorn cane tapping a steady rhythm on the stone as they moved through the parting crowd. Tam ran to them, her boots slipping on the marble.

Finch stopped. She took both of Tam’s hands. Her own fingers trembled, a fine, constant vibration, but her grip was firm. She held Tam’s steady hands in her shaking ones.

"I cannot draw a straight line any more," Finch said softly. Her voice was gravel and honey. "But look. I have left one behind."

Tam looked at the silver pen in her hand. She looked at the scroll. She looked at Finch, who was smiling with her eyes, her face crinkling like a piece of old paper.

Tam cried. She cried into the lavender scarf, which smelled of hawthorn and dried ink. Finch patted her hair with her free hand, the cane tapping gently against the floor, keeping time, keeping her there.
pages.image: Master Finch, a tall thin woman with white hair and a lavender scarf, holds the hands of a freckled girl with a black braid, her face kind and smiling, while a silver pen rests on the marble floor between them.

pages.text:
Later, on the steps, the city noise rushed up to meet them. Gulls screamed overhead, and carriage wheels clattered against the cobblestones. Lucan found Tam sitting on the lowest stone, the silver pen tucked safely into her coat pocket.

He stood there, shifting his weight from one boot to the other. He looked uncomfortable, like a cat that had accidentally walked into a sunbeam.

"I have never had a friend," he said, finally, "who didn't want something from my father."

Tam looked up. She wiped her nose on her sleeve, a very un-noble gesture.

"I only want your gold compass back," she said.

Lucan stared at her. Then, slowly, the corners of his mouth turned up. It was a real grin, wide and a little crooked, nothing like his usual polite smile.

"No," he said, reaching up to untangle the chain. He held it out to her, then pulled it back. "No, I think I will keep it. For now."

He extended his hand. She took it. It was a deal.
pages.image: Lucan Ravel stands on stone steps, offering a gold compass on a chain to Tamsin Marrow, who sits below him; both are smiling, the city of Verrin and its bridges visible in the background.
